claims.text: A checkpoint transfers transactions from the WAL file back into the original database file.
claims.quote: Moving the WAL file transactions back into the database is called a " checkpoint ".

claims.text: By default, SQLite checkpoints when a COMMIT makes the WAL at least 1000 pages or when the last connection to the database closes.
claims.quote: By default, SQLite will automatically checkpoint whenever a COMMIT occurs that causes the WAL file to be 1000 pages or more in size, or when the last database connection on a database file closes.

claims.text: Applications can adjust the automatic threshold, disable automatic checkpoints, or run checkpoints during idle periods or in another thread or process.
claims.quote: But if they want to, applications can adjust the automatic checkpoint threshold. Or they can turn off the automatic checkpoints and run checkpoints during idle moments or in a separate thread or process.

claims.text: sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint configures a checkpoint after a COMMIT when the WAL has at least N frames.
claims.quote: The sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint(D,N) is a wrapper around sqlite3_wal_hook() that causes any database on database connection D to automatically checkpoint after committing a transaction if there are N or more frames in the write-ahead log file.

claims.text: Passing zero or a negative N disables automatic checkpoints.
claims.quote: Passing zero or a negative value as the N parameter disables automatic checkpoints entirely.

claims.text: Checkpoints initiated by the automatic mechanism use PASSIVE mode.
claims.quote: All checkpoints initiated by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() and by the automatic checkpoint mechanism are PASSIVE.

claims.text: An application can initiate a checkpoint through either checkpoint API using any writable database connection.
claims.quote: An application can initiate a checkpoint using any writable database connection on the database simply by invoking sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() or sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2().

claims.text: PASSIVE checkpoints as many frames as possible without waiting for readers or writers, and syncs the database if all log frames were checkpointed.
claims.quote: Checkpoint as many frames as possible without waiting for any database readers or writers to finish, then sync the database file if all frames in the log were checkpointed.

claims.text: PASSIVE mode never invokes the busy-handler callback.
claims.quote: The busy-handler callback is never invoked in the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE mode. On the other hand, passive mode might leave the checkpoint unfinished if there are concurrent readers or writers.

claims.text: PASSIVE may leave a checkpoint unfinished when readers or writers are concurrent.
claims.quote: On the other hand, passive mode might leave the checkpoint unfinished if there are concurrent readers or writers.

claims.text: FULL waits until there is no writer and all readers use the most recent database snapshot.
claims.quote: This mode blocks (it invokes the busy-handler callback ) until there is no database writer and all readers are reading from the most recent database snapshot.

claims.text: After that wait, FULL checkpoints all log frames and syncs the database file.
claims.quote: It then checkpoints all frames in the log file and syncs the database file.

claims.text: FULL blocks new writers while pending but allows new readers to continue unimpeded.
claims.quote: This mode blocks new database writers while it is pending, but new database readers are allowed to continue unimpeded.

claims.text: RESTART works like FULL, then waits until all readers read only from the database file.
claims.quote: This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL with the addition that after checkpointing the log file it blocks (calls the busy-handler callback ) until all readers are reading from the database file only.

claims.text: After RESTART completes, the next writer restarts the log from its beginning.
claims.quote: This ensures that the next writer will restart the log file from the beginning.

claims.text: The interface description says RESTART does not impede readers while it is pending.
claims.quote: Like SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL, this mode blocks new database writer attempts while it is pending, but does not impede readers.

claims.text: TRUNCATE works like RESTART and truncates the log to zero bytes before a successful return.
claims.quote: This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART with the addition that it also truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior to a successful return.

claims.text: NOOP checkpoints zero frames and is used to access the returned log and checkpoint counts.
claims.quote: This mode always checkpoints zero frames. The only reason to invoke a NOOP checkpoint is to access the values returned by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() via output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt.

claims.text: All checkpoint calls take an exclusive checkpoint lock; a concurrent checkpoint causes SQLITE_BUSY.
claims.quote: All calls obtain an exclusive "checkpoint" lock on the database file. If any other process is running a checkpoint operation at the same time, the lock cannot be obtained and SQLITE_BUSY is returned.

claims.text: If the writer lock is unavailable and a busy handler is configured, SQLite invokes it and retries until the handler returns zero or the lock is obtained.
claims.quote: If the writer lock cannot be obtained immediately, and a busy-handler is configured, it is invoked and the writer lock retried until either the busy-handler returns 0 or the lock is successfully obtained.

claims.text: A checkpoint can run alongside readers but must stop at a WAL page beyond any current reader's end mark.
claims.quote: A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers, however the checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader.

claims.text: The checkpoint remembers its progress and resumes transferring WAL content from that point on its next invocation.
claims.quote: The checkpoint remembers (in the wal-index) how far it got and will resume transferring content from the WAL to the database from where it left off on the next invocation.

claims.text: A long-running read transaction can prevent a checkpointer from making progress.
claims.quote: Thus a long-running read transaction can prevent a checkpointer from making progress.

claims.text: The writer rewinds the WAL only after all its content has been transferred and synced and no readers are using it.
claims.quote: if the entire WAL has been transferred into the database and synced and if no readers are making use of the WAL, then the writer will rewind the WAL back to the beginning

claims.text: A checkpoint normally recycles the WAL by overwriting it from the beginning rather than truncating it; journal_size_limit is an exception.
claims.quote: The checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file (unless the journal_size_limit pragma is set). Instead, it merely causes SQLite to start overwriting the WAL file from the beginning.

claims.text: Disabling automatic checkpoints removes the default mechanism that prevents excessive WAL growth.
claims.quote: If an application disables the automatic checkpoint, then there is nothing to prevent the WAL file from growing excessively.

claims.text: If overlapping readers always leave at least one active reader, checkpoints cannot complete and the WAL can grow without bound.
claims.quote: However, if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers and there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.

claims.text: Reader gaps, with checkpoint attempts during those periods, can avoid this starvation scenario.
claims.quote: This scenario can be avoided by ensuring that there are "reader gaps": times when no processes are reading from the database and that checkpoints are attempted during those times.

claims.text: The WAL guide says manual RESTART or TRUNCATE checkpoints ensure completion before returning.
claims.quote: In applications with many concurrent readers, one might also consider running manual checkpoints with the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART or SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE option which will ensure that the checkpoint runs to completion before returning.

claims.text: The WAL guide warns that readers might block while RESTART or TRUNCATE is running.
claims.quote: The disadvantage of using SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART and SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE is that readers might block while the checkpoint is running.

claims.text: Checkpointing requires syncing the WAL before transferring its content and syncing the database before resetting the WAL.
claims.quote: The WAL must be synced to persistent storage prior to moving content from the WAL into the database and the database file must be synced prior to resetting the WAL.

claims.text: Read performance declines as the WAL grows because readers must check the WAL for content.
claims.quote: read performance deteriorates as the WAL file grows in size since each reader must check the WAL file for the content

claims.text: The WAL guide describes checkpoint frequency as a tradeoff between average read and write performance.
claims.quote: Notice too that there is a tradeoff between average read performance and average write performance.

claims.text: With PRAGMA synchronous set to NORMAL, the checkpoint is the only operation that issues an I/O barrier or sync operation.
claims.quote: Note that with PRAGMA synchronous set to NORMAL, the checkpoint is the only operation to issue an I/O barrier or sync operation (fsync() on unix or FlushFileBuffers() on windows).

claims.text: The guide says transactions in this configuration may roll back after a power failure or hard reset.
claims.quote: The downside to this configuration is that transactions are no longer durable and might rollback following a power failure or hard reset.

limitations: The packet contains three primary SQLite documentation pages from one origin, so it does not provide independent-origin corroboration.

The WAL guide says readers might block during RESTART or TRUNCATE, while the checkpoint API page says RESTART does not impede readers and describes TRUNCATE as adding truncation to RESTART; the packet does not reconcile these statements.
The automatic-checkpoint documentation uses both pages and frames when describing thresholds, and the packet does not explain that terminology difference.
The packet does not establish version history or disagreements beyond the reader-blocking statements above.
